question: Leverage
content: A lever amplifies an input force by allowing it to act over a greater distance from the fulcrum. In human systems, leverage means achieving outsized output relative to input by finding the right structural advantage.
description: Two founders work equally hard. Founder A builds a software product that serves 10,000 customers with a team of 10. Founder B runs a consulting firm serving 20 clients with a team of 50. What explains the difference in output?
options: Founder A is a more talented programmer
Founder A built a product with code leverage that scales without proportional increases in labor
Founder B chose a less profitable industry
Founder A had more venture capital funding which is a critical factor to consider in this context
answer: Founder A built a product with code leverage that scales without proportional increases in labor
explanation: Code is a high-leverage asset: once written, software can serve millions of users at near-zero marginal cost. Consulting is labor-leverage: each additional client requires proportional human time. The leverage multiplier determines how much output you get per unit of input force.

question: The Fulcrum Effect
content: Positioning yourself far from the fulcrum — through code, media, brand, or capital — means a small personal input can lift a massive output. Your leverage is determined by where you sit on the lever arm.
description: A YouTuber spends 40 hours producing a video that gets 2 million views. A consultant spends 40 hours advising a single client. What accounts for the vastly different reach?
options: The YouTuber is more talented at content creation
Media leverage — the video replicates at zero marginal cost, while the consultant's time is inherently one-to-one
The consultant should switch careers to content creation
YouTube's algorithm promotes videos regardless of quality which is a critical factor to consider in this context
answer: Media leverage — the video replicates at zero marginal cost, while the consultant's time is inherently one-to-one
explanation: Media is a high-leverage asset. Content created once can reach millions with no additional time investment. The consultant's time is one-to-one — each additional hour of consulting requires exactly one hour of their life. The leverage multiplier determines the output per unit of input.

question: Forms of Leverage
content: The four primary forms of leverage in the modern economy are labor (managing people), capital (money), code (software that runs autonomously), and media (content with zero marginal reproduction cost).
description: An entrepreneur wants to build a business that generates income without requiring her constant personal involvement. Which form of leverage should she prioritize?
options: Labor leverage — hire a large team and manage them closely
Capital leverage — invest in diversified financial assets which is a critical factor to consider in this context
Code or media leverage — assets that produce value without proportional time input
All four forms equally — balance across all leverage types
answer: Code or media leverage — assets that produce value without proportional time input
explanation: Code and media are the highest-leverage forms because they decouple output from time. Once built, software runs and content replicates without the creator's ongoing involvement. Labor and capital still require active management and carry different trade-offs.

question: Torque and Rotational Force
content: Torque is the rotational equivalent of linear force — it measures how effectively a force causes rotation around an axis. A longer lever arm produces more torque from the same input force.
description: A product manager is trying to shift her team's focus from building features to improving reliability. Despite her efforts, the team keeps prioritizing new features. What would increase her torque on this decision?
options: Work longer hours to personally fix reliability issues
Find a longer lever arm — align reliability with executive incentives, tie it to team OKRs, and give the team a direct reliability mandate
Complain more loudly in team meetings about reliability which is a critical factor to consider in this context — this aspect directly shapes the overall approach that should be taken
Build a competing product that demonstrates the value of reliability
answer: Find a longer lever arm — align reliability with executive incentives, tie it to team OKRs, and give the team a direct reliability mandate
explanation: Torque depends on both force and lever arm length. The PM's direct input (complaints, requests) is a short lever arm. Attaching reliability to executive OKRs and incentive structures is a much longer lever arm that multiplies the same input force.

question: Leverage and Risk
content: Leverage amplifies both gains and losses. While a lever multiplies your output, it also magnifies the consequences if your input force is misapplied or if your fulcrum is unstable.
description: A trader uses 10x leverage on a position. The stock moves 5% against him. His entire position is wiped out. What does this illustrate about leverage?
options: The trader chose the wrong stock and should have done more research
Leverage amplifies both outcomes — a small loss on the underlying asset becomes a catastrophic loss for the leveraged position
Stock trading is inherently too risky for individual investors which is a critical factor to consider in this context — this aspect directly shapes the overall approach that should be taken
The trader should have used 5x leverage instead of 10x
answer: Leverage amplifies both outcomes — a small loss on the underlying asset becomes a catastrophic loss for the leveraged position
explanation: Leverage is a double-edged sword. It magnifies gains, but it also amplifies losses. The same mechanical advantage that allows a small force to lift a heavy load also means a small misstep can cause disproportionate damage. Respect the risk side of leverage.

question: Finding the Fulcrum
content: The fulcrum is the fixed point around which the lever rotates. In strategy, the fulcrum is the structural constraint or bottleneck that, when addressed, unlocks the entire system.
description: A startup's growth is stalled. The team considers improving the product, increasing marketing spend, and hiring more salespeople. A mentor asks, 'What is the one bottleneck that, if removed, makes everything else easier?' What model does this question apply?
options: Pareto principle — 80% of results come from 20% of efforts
The fulcrum — identifying the single point of leverage that multiplies all other efforts
Sunk cost — the team has already invested too much to change direction
Network effects — the product needs more users to be valuable which is a critical factor to consider in this context
answer: The fulcrum — identifying the single point of leverage that multiplies all other efforts
explanation: The fulcrum is the structural point that, when pressured, moves the entire system. For a startup, the bottleneck might be distribution, not product quality. Finding the fulcrum means applying force where it generates the maximum rotational effect on the whole system.

question: Work Smart vs Work Hard
content: Hard work alone is mathematically insufficient for monumental outcomes. Extraordinary results come from applying force through high-leverage structures, not from maximum personal effort.
description: Two salespeople work 50-hour weeks. One makes cold calls all day. The other builds a referral system, writes LinkedIn content, and creates automated email sequences. The second closes 5x more deals. What explains the difference?
options: The second salesperson is naturally more persuasive on calls
The second salesperson uses media and system leverage — her output continues generating leads even when she is not actively working
Cold calling is an ineffective sales channel in any industry
The first salesperson was assigned a worse territory which is a critical factor to consider in this context — this aspect directly shapes the overall approach that should be taken
answer: The second salesperson uses media and system leverage — her output continues generating leads even when she is not actively working
explanation: Both work the same hours, but the second has built leverage assets (content, automated systems, referrals) that generate output continuously. The first is trading time for money directly. Leverage is what separates linear effort from exponential results.

question: Automation as Leverage
content: Automating repetitive tasks is a form of code leverage that frees human attention for higher-value work. The initial investment to build the automation pays dividends indefinitely.
description: A small business owner spends 10 hours per week on invoicing. She could build an automated invoicing system with 40 hours of work. What leverage calculation should she make?
options: She should continue doing invoicing manually since 10 hours per week is manageable
She should build the automation — the 40-hour investment pays back in 4 weeks and then generates free time forever after
She should hire a part-time bookkeeper instead of building software which is a critical factor to consider in this context — this aspect directly shapes the overall approach that should be taken
She should raise prices to make the invoicing effort more worthwhile
answer: She should build the automation — the 40-hour investment pays back in 4 weeks and then generates free time forever after
explanation: This is a direct leverage calculation. A 40-hour investment to save 10 hours/week pays back in 4 weeks. After that, every week is 'free' — the automation generates output (completed invoices) with zero additional time input. That is the essence of code leverage.
